prompt: Distinguish between transverse and longitudinal waves, giving one example of each.
markscheme: Transverse: oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer, e.g. light, waves on a string **(A1)**; longitudinal: oscillations parallel to the direction of energy transfer, e.g. sound **(A1)**

prompt:
**(a)** Calculate the wavelength of a 100 MHz radio wave ($c=3.0\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$). **[1]**

**(b)** Crests 0.40 m apart pass a point at a rate of 5 per second. Calculate the wave speed. **[1]**
Describe the nature of a sound wave in air, and explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
markscheme: A longitudinal wave: air molecules oscillate parallel to the direction of travel **(A1)**, forming compressions (high pressure) and rarefactions (low pressure) **(A1)**. It is a mechanical wave that needs particles to pass on the oscillation, and a vacuum has none **(R1)**

prompt: Which statement about electromagnetic waves is **incorrect**?
options: They consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields.
They can travel through a vacuum.
Gamma rays travel faster than radio waves in a vacuum.
markscheme: **D.** All EM waves travel at the same speed $c$ in a vacuum; they differ in frequency and wavelength. They are transverse oscillations of electric and magnetic fields, and can be polarised.

prompt: State two differences between sound waves and light waves.
markscheme: Any two **(A2)**: sound needs a medium, light does not; sound is longitudinal, light is transverse (so only light can be polarised); light travels about $10^{6}$ times faster; sound travels faster in solids, light slower in denser media.
